card: Paper card. Question: What are the optimization strategies of high-entropy alloys for electrocatalytic applications?. System: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) composed of five or more equiatomic or near-equiatomic components. Processing: Various methods including carbon thermal shock, moving bed pyrolysis, magnetron sputtering, electrodeposition, and dealloying. Findings: HEAs have a highly disordered structure and a wide range of composition modulation, showing excellent performance in mechanical properties, magnetic properties, and electrocatalysis; HEAs have abundant active sites, high selectivity, and high stability, making them ideal catalytic materials in electrocatalytic reactions; The high entropy effect, slow diffusion effect, lattice distortion effect, and cocktail effect of HEAs contribute to their unique properties and performance; Element regulation, defect regulation, and strain engineering are effective strategies for optimizing HEA catalysts. Mechanism: The high entropy effect, slow diffusion effect, lattice distortion effect, and cocktail effect of HEAs contribute to their unique properties and performance. Future work: Further research is needed to explore the potential of HEAs in electrocatalytic applications and to develop more efficient synthesis methods and optimization strategies. Quote: "High-entropy alloys (HEAs) are expected to become one of the most promising functional materials in the field of electrocatalysis"

Paper card. Question: How can high-entropy alloys (HEAs) be optimized for electrocatalytic applications?. System: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) with various compositions, such as CrMnFeCoNi, CuMnFeCoNi, and MnFeCoNi. Findings: 1.0; 2.0; 3.0; HEAs have shown potential in electrocatalytic research due to their excellent combined properties; The introduction of Cu causes the original ORR performance to deteriorate, while the introduction of Cr improves the original catalytic performance; The randomly distributed metal elements promote the formation of a large number of active centers on the surface of HEAs. Mechanism: The inherent surface complexity of HEAs can provide nearly continuous adsorption energy and increase the proportion of active sites. Limitations: There are still many challenges in the research of the catalytic mechanism and practical applications. Future work: The combination of theory and experiment is very important to understand the catalytic mechanisms of HEAs. Quote: "HEAs have shown more and more obvious potential in electrocatalytic research due to their excellent combined properties"

card: Paper card. Question: How can the miscibility gap in bimetallic Co-Mo alloys be overcome to create tunable, highly active catalysts for ammonia decomposition using earth-abundant elements?. System: Quinary CoMoFeNiCu high-entropy alloy nanoparticles (general composition CoxMoyFe10Ni10Cu10 where x + y = 70) and control samples of bimetallic Co-Mo and monometallic Ru. Processing: Carbothermal shock technique involving flash heating and cooling of metal precursors on oxygenated carbon nanofibers; temperature reached 2000–2300 K with ramping rates on the order of 10^5 K s−1 and shock duration of ~55 ms. Test conditions: Ammonia decomposition in a plug flow reactor at 250–600 °C using 5 vol% NH3 (and 100 vol% NH3 for specific tests) at a gas hourly space velocity (GHSV) of 36 L gcat−1 h−1. Findings: HEA-Co25Mo45 achieved a mass-specific reaction rate of 22.1 gNH3 gmetals−1 h−1 at 500 °C, representing an improvement factor of ~19 versus bimetallic Co-Mo and ~3 versus Ru.; The most active catalyst, HEA-Co25Mo45, reached 50% NH3 conversion (T50) at 422 °C, compared to 600 °C for Ru and 600 °C for bimetallic Co-Mo.; The apparent activation energy (Eapp) varied from 64.7 kJ mol−1 for the most active HEA-Co25Mo45 to 123.1 kJ mol−1 for the least active HEA-Co55Mo15.; Nitrogen desorption energy (ΔEN) for HEA-Co25Mo45 was ~79 kJ mol−1, which is very close to the value for Ru (84 kJ mol−1).; Catalytic activity exhibited a volcano-type behavior with respect to nitrogen adsorption energy, peaking at an optimal ΔEN of ~79 kJ mol−1.; The HEA-Co25Mo45 catalyst showed negligible degradation after ~50 hours of continuous operation at 500 °C.; For pure NH3 decomposition, HEA-Co55Mo15 achieved an improvement factor of ~118 versus bimetallic Co-Mo and ~40 versus Ru.; Atomistic modeling confirmed a single solid-solution phase with δ = 5.4% and ΔHmix = 0.65 kJ mol−1, showing no phase segregation up to 1000 K.. Mechanism: The high catalytic activity is attributed to the robust tuning of surface nitrogen binding strength via the Co/Mo ratio; the optimal activity arises from a tradeoff where Co-rich catalysts bind N too weakly (limiting dehydrogenation) and Mo-rich catalysts bind N too strongly (limiting N2 desorption), with the HEA composition allowing access to the optimal intermediate binding energy (~79 kJ mol−1) predicted by the Sabatier principle.. Limitations: The text notes that the peak intensities in XRD patterns are low due to the much smaller particle sizes compared to previously reported HEAs, and that the bimetallic Co-Mo catalysts are constrained by large miscibility gaps in their phase diagram.. Future work: The authors propose designing practical reactors with cascaded catalyst layers having gradually changing nitrogen binding strengths to match the varying concentration of NH3 along the flow, which can be readily achieved by varying the Co/Mo ratios in HEA catalysts.. Quote: "Quinary CoMoFeNiCu nanoparticles are synthesized in a single solid-solution phase with robust control over the Co/Mo atomic ratio, including those ratios considered to be immiscible according to the Co-Mo bimetallic phase diagram."

card: Paper card. Question: How can uniformly dispersed high-entropy alloy nanoparticles (HEA-NPs) be synthesized on granular supports (e.g., carbon, Al2O3, zeolite) without phase separation, overcoming the limitations of conventional fixed-bed pyrolysis?. System: Denary (MnCoNiCuRhPdSnIrPtAu), quinary (FeCoPdIrPt, CuPdSnPtAu), and other multi-element (up to 10 elements) HEA-NPs supported on graphene oxide (GO), carbon black, γ-Al2O3, and zeolite (Permutit). Processing: Fast moving bed pyrolysis (FMBP) following wet impregnation: Metal chlorides coordinated with 1,10-Phenanthroline loaded on supports; quartz boat pushed into a 923 K furnace zone at 20 cm s−1 (reaching 923 K within 5 s); annealing for 120 min at 923 K under Ar (100 sccm) or H2 (100 sccm) for oxide supports. Test conditions: Electrochemical hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) in 1 M KOH (pH 13.8) at 10 mA cm−2 and 100 mA cm−2; stability tested via chronopotentiometry for 150 h; structural characterization via HR-STEM, HAADF-STEM, EDX, XRD, XPS, and ICP-OES. Findings: HEA-NPs achieved a narrow size distribution of ~2 nm up to denary compositions at 923 K; FMBP ensures simultaneous pyrolysis of mixed precursors, preventing phase separation unlike fixed-bed pyrolysis (FBP) which yields phase-separated alloys; FeCoPdIrPt@GO exhibited an overpotential of 42 mV at 10 mA cm−2, lower than commercial Pt/C (64 mV); Mass activity of FeCoPdIrPt@GO at 100 mV overpotential was 9.1 mA μgPt, 26 times higher than Pt/C (0.35 mA μgPt); Long-term stability of 150 h maintained at 10 mA cm−2 with no obvious change in morphology or composition; Atomic ratio error in synthesized alloys was below 15%, confirmed by EDX and ICP-OES; Tafel slope for FeCoPdIrPt was 82 mV dec−1, indicating the fastest kinetics among tested samples. Mechanism: The rapid heating to 923 K within 5 s creates high supersaturation of monomers, leading to a small critical nucleus radius (r* = 0.313 nm) and low critical excess free energy (ΔGr* = 2.54 × 10−20 J). This thermodynamically favors the formation of small, homogeneous nuclei clusters without phase separation, whereas slower heating (FBP/SMBP) results in larger nuclei and phase segregation due to higher ΔGr*.. Limitations: The text notes that HEA-NPs with low loading (3 wt%) were too small for clear EDX mapping, requiring higher loading (10 wt%) for elemental analysis; also, annealing times of 30 min led to carbon wrapping, while 180 min caused significant particle growth.. Future work: The authors propose a scalable method for production of supported HEA-NPs and suggest the strategy opens a venue for synthesizing alloys with tunable compositions for applications in catalysis, chemical sensing, biology, and energy conversion.. Quote: "Fast moving bed pyrolysis strategy ensures the mixed metal precursors rapidly and simultaneously pyrolyzed at high temperatures, resulting in nuclei with a small size."

card: Paper card. Question: How can PtRu-based high-entropy alloys be synthesized with subnanometer dimensions and tailored morphologies to achieve high activity, stability, and CO resistance for alkaline hydrogen oxidation reaction (HOR)?. System: PtRuNiCoFeMo high-entropy alloy subnanometer nanowires (SNWs) with composition Pt/Ru/Ni/Co/Fe/Mo = 29.6/9.3/15.2/15.6/12.2/18.1 (SEM-EDS) or 28.5/6.8/18.6/15.2/10.7/20.2 (ICP-OES). Processing: Synthesis via solvothermal reduction: metal precursors (Pt(acac)2, Ru(acac)3, Ni(acac)2, Co(acac)3, Fe(acac)3, Mo(CO)6), glucose (reducing agent), and STAB (structure-directing agent) dissolved in oleylamine (OAm), heated at 210 °C for 5 h, followed by centrifugation and washing with cyclohexane/ethanol (1:9 v/v). Test conditions: Alkaline HOR in 0.1 M KOH solution purged with H2; accelerated durability test (ADT) for 2000 cycles between -0.1 V and 0.4 V vs. RHE at 500 mV s-1; CO poisoning tests in 0.1 M KOH with 1000 ppm CO/H2; chronoamperometry at 100 mV vs. RHE. Findings: Mass activity of HEA SNWs/C reached 6.75 A mgPt+Ru−1, which is 4.1 times higher than commercial PtRu/C (1.65 A mgPt+Ru−1) and 19.8 times higher than Pt/C (0.34 A mgPt+Ru−1); Specific activity of HEA SNWs/C was 8.96 mA cm−2, 2.4 times higher than PtRu/C (3.77 mA cm−2) and 18.7 times higher than Pt/C (0.48 mA cm−2); Only 6.2% loss in mass activity was observed after 2000 ADT cycles for HEA SNWs/C, compared to 20.6%, 31.5%, and 35.3% losses for HEA NPs/C, PtRu/C, and Pt/C respectively; In the presence of 1000 ppm CO, the limiting current density of HEA SNWs/C decreased by only 5.4% at 100 mV vs. RHE, whereas PtRu/C and Pt/C decreased by 21.3% and 22.7%; Chronoamperometry showed HEA SNWs/C activity decreased by 26.4% after 2000 s in 1000 ppm CO, while PtRu/C decreased by 82.9% and Pt/C completely deactivated after 1130 s; The d-band center of HEA SNWs/C shifted upwards to -3.835 eV compared to -3.732 eV for HEA NPs/C, weakening H* adsorption and facilitating OH* adsorption; DFT calculations revealed the energy barrier for H2O formation on HEA surface was as low as 0.08 eV, much lower than 0.57 eV for Pt and 0.27 eV for PtRu; The binding strength of H* on HEA SNWs/C was weakened to an appropriate level near 0 eV, while OH* binding on Ru was moderate at nearly -0.6 eV. Mechanism: Strong electronic interactions between different metal sites in HEA SNWs regulate the binding strength of protons and hydroxyls; Co and Ni sites maintain stable valence states due to pinning effects by Fe and Mo, while Pt and Ru sites modulate overall electroactivity; the upshifted d-band center weakens H* adsorption and facilitates OH* adsorption, and the low energy barrier for H2O formation (0.08 eV) enables rapid desorption and superior HOR activity. Limitations: The text does not explicitly state limitations of the study, though it notes that controlled synthesis of PtRu-based HEAs with tailored morphologies remains a general challenge in the field. Future work: The authors propose that the work provides a viable synthetic route for fabricating Pt-based HEA subnano/nano materials and promotes fundamental research on catalysis and beyond. Quote: "The mass and specific activities of HEA SNWs/C reach 6.75 A mgPt+Ru−1 and 8.96 mA cm−2, respectively"

card: Paper card. Question: How can the design principles of metastable β-Ti alloys be converged with high-entropy/medium-entropy alloys to achieve both high yield strength and low elastic modulus for biomedical implants?. System: Ti-Zr-Nb-Ta-Mo, Ti-Zr-Nb-Ta, Ti-Zr-Hf-Nb-Ta, Ti-V-Mo, Ti-V-Zr-Mo, and Ti-rich variants (e.g., Ti65-Zr20-Nb10-Mo5, Ti35-Zr27.5-Hf27.5-Nb5-Ta5). Processing: Casting (as-cast), annealing (e.g., 1000 °C for 168 h), and thermodynamic simulation using FactSage, Pandat, and Thermo-Calc to adjust compositions for phase stability and segregation reduction. Test conditions: Potentiodynamic polarization in simulated body fluid, compression and tensile testing, cell culture tests (osteoblasts), X-ray diffraction (XRD), SAED-TEM, and EPMA-WDS mapping. Findings: Equiatomic Ti-Zr-Nb-Ta-Mo HEA exhibited a compressive yield strength of 1330 MPa but suffered from severe dendritic segregation and a high elastic modulus.; Ti-Zr-Nb-Ta MEA (quaternary) achieved a compressive strain of 48 ± 6% and yield strength >1000 MPa, surpassing Ti-6Al-4V (970 MPa).; Ti65-Zr20-Nb10-Mo5 alloy showed the lowest elastic modulus (86 GPa) among Ti-rich MEAs and a yield strength of 1381 MPa.; Metastable Ti65-Zr18-Nb16-Mo1 ([Mo]eq ≈ 10) achieved high yield strength (>1100 MPa) and a lower elastic modulus (~60 GPa).; Ti45-Zr45-Nb5-Ta5 MEA (VEC = 4.18) exhibited a low elastic modulus of 57 GPa.; Increasing Ti content in Tix-Nb-Mo-Ta-W HEAs increased yield strength by 31% (Ti1 vs Ti0.25) and improved compressive deformability.; Ti1.4-Zr1.4-Nb0.6-Ta0.6-Mo0.6 HEA showed osteoblasts with more pseudopodia and longer focal adhesions compared to commercially pure Ti.. Mechanism: The authors argue that reducing the valence electron concentration (VEC) to 4.0–4.2 or the Mo equivalent ([Mo]eq) to below 10 wt% induces a metastable β-phase, which lowers the elastic modulus. Simultaneously, the high-entropy effects (lattice distortion, solid solution strengthening) and Ti-rich compositions enhance yield strength. Reducing the atomic size misfit (δ) and mixing enthalpy (ΔHmix) near zero minimizes compositional segregation and prevents intermetallic formation, thereby improving ductility and corrosion resistance.. Limitations: Severe compositional segregation persists in many equiatomic and non-equiatomic HEAs/MEAs, leading to high elastic modulus, reduced ductility, and decreased corrosion resistance. The Ms theory may not be applicable to HEAs/MEAs, and some alloys with high Ti content still exhibit segregation. The presence of Laves phases or secondary BCC phases can adversely affect mechanical properties.. Future work: Developing metastable β HEAs/MEAs that combine high strength and low modulus; surface modification of Ti-containing HEAs to induce bioactivity (e.g., anodization, hydroxyapatite deposition); further investigation into the relationship between thermodynamic parameters and modulus; and reducing segregation through optimized composition design.. Quote: "To satisfy the demands of biomedical implants, researchers have sought to synthesize the strengths of high-entropy alloys and metastable β-Ti alloys, culminating in the development of metastable high-entropy/medium-entropy alloys that manifest both high strength and a low elastic modulus."

card: Paper card. Question: How to rapidly design low-cost Co-free Al-Cr-Fe-Ni FCC/B2-structured eutectic medium entropy alloys (EMEAs) with excellent mechanical and corrosion properties?. System: Al-Cr-Fe-Ni system, specifically AlCr1.18FeNi2.8 and AlCrFe1.46Ni2.5 alloys. Processing: Vacuum arc melting under pure argon atmosphere; raw materials >99.9 wt% purity; remelted at least five times; solidified in a water-cooled copper hearth (18 mm diameter, 12 mm thickness). Test conditions: Compressive tests at 1 × 10−3 s−1 strain rate; electrochemical tests in 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution at 25 °C; potentiodynamic polarization scan rate 1 mV/min; EIS from 105 to 10−2 Hz. Findings: Mathematical rules established: c ≥ 1.0, 4.38a + 4.28b + 3.97c ≈ 20.55, and c − a ˃ 1.0.; Both alloys exhibit lamellar eutectic microstructure with FCC and ordered B2 (B2) phases.; Volume ratio of B2 to FCC phase (VB2/VFCC) is 0.605 for AlCr1.18FeNi2.8 and 0.679 for AlCrFe1.46Ni2.5.; Yield stress higher than 500 MPa and compressive fracture strength higher than 2450 MPa.; Fracture strain > 40% for both alloys.; AlCr1.18FeNi2.8 shows better corrosion resistance with Ecorr of −436 mV and Icorr of 7.42 μA∙cm−2.; Cr-rich spherical nanoparticles segregate within the B2 phase matrix.; L12 nanoprecipitates are found within the FCC phase of AlCrFe1.46Ni2.5.. Mechanism: The unique lamellar microstructure allows coordinated deformation: soft FCC phase undergoes initial plastic deformation while hard B2 phase remains elastic, piling up dislocations at interfaces; Cr-rich BCC nanoprecipitates further hinder dislocation movement, improving strength and strain-hardening. Better corrosion resistance in AlCr1.18FeNi2.8 is attributed to the higher volume fraction of the FCC phase and higher nickel content.. Limitations: The text notes that traditional trial-and-error methods are time-consuming and have low success rates, though the proposed rule addresses this; no specific limitations of the current study's results are explicitly stated by the authors beyond the general challenge of industrial application for Co-containing alloys which this work aims to solve.. Future work: The authors state that the established rule has great potential in the composition design of EHEAs and imply further application of this rule to design more alloys, but do not explicitly list specific future experiments in the 'future work' section.. Quote: "The mathematical formulas are c ≥ 1.0, 4.38a + 4.28b + 3.97c ≈ 20.55, and c − a ˃ 1.0."

card: Paper card. Question: How does the biocompatibility of a Ti-rich medium-entropy alloy (Ti65M) compare to a Ti-alloy (TNSM) and commercially pure titanium (CP-Ti) regarding glioblastoma astrocytoma cell viability, morphology, and gene expression?. System: Ti65-Zr18-Nb16-Mo1 (Ti65M), Ti-13Nb-7Sn-4Mo (TNSM), and commercially pure titanium (CP-Ti). Processing: Arc-melting and casting system (A-028, Dawn Shine, New Taipei City, Taiwan); samples cut into discs (10 mm diameter, 1 mm height); surfaces abraded to #1500 silicon carbide papers; cleaned ultrasonically with alcohol, acetone, and deionized water. Test conditions: U-87 MG glioblastoma astrocytoma cells (1 × 10^4 cells) seeded on 1.2 cm diameter samples; incubated for 24 h, then replated for an additional 24 h prior to MTT tests; extracts tested via PBS wash; contact angles measured with 1μL deionized water; XRD (40 kV, 40 mA, 2θ = 20–90°); AFM (5 × 5 μm2 scanning range). Findings: Ti65M exhibited the highest hardness (366.5 ± 3.6 HV) and lowest average roughness (38 ± 8 nm), while CP-Ti had the lowest hardness (172.3 ± 4.4 HV) and highest roughness (94 ± 26 nm).; All three materials were hydrophilic, with CP-Ti having the lowest contact angle (46.0 ± 0.9°) compared to Ti65M (54.3 ± 2.0°).; Cell viability on Ti65M and TNSM (β structures) was considerably higher than on CP-Ti (α' structure), with viability decreasing as Ti content increased.; U-87 MG cells showed the highest number of dendrites and axons on Ti65M, with significantly fewer observed on TNSM and CP-Ti.; Expression of ERK was reduced on TNSM and CP-Ti substrates compared to Ti65M, potentially causing lower cell migration and proliferation.; Higher expression of p53 and NFkβ was observed in U-87 MG cells on CP-Ti compared to other alloys, suggesting CP-Ti may induce apoptosis.; All extract viabilities exceeded 90%, indicating low indirect cytotoxicity for all three materials.. Mechanism: The authors propose that the superior biocompatibility of Ti65M is related to its high content of Zr and Nb elements, which are highly biocompatible and exhibit low cytotoxicity. Additionally, the metastable β-phase structure and high hardness improve wear resistance, preventing accelerated release of metal ions. The lower expression of p53 on Ti65M compared to CP-Ti suggests reduced apoptosis, while higher expression of growth factor pathway genes (RAS, ERK, S6) on Ti65M correlates with increased cell growth and migration.. Limitations: The authors state that the mechanisms connecting surface roughness and hydrophilicity to cellular adhesion, growth, autophagy, and differentiation are not yet clear. They also note that phase structure alone is insufficient to explain viability differences and that further investigation of corrosion resistance is needed.. Future work: The authors propose that increased cell migration on Ti65M is a subject for further study and that further investigation of the corrosion resistance of Ti65M and TNSM will be reported in future studies.. Quote: "Ti65M has an ultra-low elastic modulus (61 GPa) due to its metastable state, which is significantly lower than those of Ti-64 (110 GPa) [] and TZNTM HEA (153 GPa) []."

card: Paper card. Question: How does thermomechanical processing (TMP) tune the microstructure and room-temperature tensile properties of a Co-rich Co35Cr25Ni15Mn15Fe10 (at%) TRIP-HEA?. System: Co35Cr25Ni15Mn15Fe10 (at%) high-entropy alloy. Processing: High-frequency induction melting and casting; forging at 1473 K; solution treatment at 1473 K for 4 h followed by water quenching (AS); hot-rolling at 1473 K to 50% reduction (HR); warm-rolling at 973 K to 50% reduction (WR); cold-rolling at 293 K to 50% reduction followed by heat treatment at 973 K for 30 min (HT1) or 1023 K for 30 min (HT2). Test conditions: Room temperature (293 K) tensile tests at a strain rate of 1 × 10−3 s−1; Vickers hardness measurement with 500 g load for 15 s. Findings: Grain size was refined from 144.4 μm in the as-solutionized (AS) sample to 1.83 μm in the HT1 sample.; Yield strength increased from 254.6 MPa (AS) to 641.3 MPa (HT2), and ultimate tensile strength increased from 702.5 MPa (AS) to 968.4 MPa (HT2).; Tensile elongation of the HT2 sample retained a satisfactory value of 68.8% despite the significant strength increase.; Nanosized Cr-rich σ-phase precipitates formed in HT samples with a volume fraction of 0.413% (HT1) and 0.681% (HT2).; The average size of precipitates was 118.8 nm for HT1 and 89 nm for HT2.; Precipitation strengthening contribution (Δσp) was estimated at 10.5 MPa for HT1 and 17.9 MPa for HT2.; Grain boundary strengthening contribution (Δσg) was calculated as 323.9 MPa for HT1 and 247.6 MPa for HT2.; The WR sample exhibited the lowest strain-hardening rate, which decreased rapidly with increasing strain.. Mechanism: Grain refinement is the primary mechanism for enhancing strength while retaining ductility, whereas nanosized incoherent precipitates provide a dual effect: they refine grains via Smith–Zener drag and block dislocation motion via Orowan strengthening, though they slightly sacrifice ductility.. Limitations: The formation of incoherent precipitates inevitably sacrifices ductility, which needs to be considered for optimizing TMPs.. Future work: The authors state that the results provide guidelines for fabricating high-performance materials and insights into the regulation of microstructure and mechanical properties of TRIP-HEAs, but do not explicitly list specific future experiments.. Quote: "The results showed that grain refinement is an effective strategy for enhancing strength while retaining satisfactory ductility."

W3092449431.title: Hot Deformation and Dynamic Recrystallization Behavior of CoCrNi and (CoCrNi)94Ti3Al3 Medium Entropy Alloys

card: Paper card. Question: How does stacking fault (SF) strengthening contribute to work hardening behavior during deformation in a low stacking fault energy (SFE) high entropy alloy, and how does it co-activate with transformation-induced plasticity (TRIP) to overcome the strength-ductility tradeoff?. System: Fe40Mn20Cr15Co20Si5 (at%) high entropy alloy with SFE ~ 6.31 mJ m−2. Processing: Vacuum induction casting to produce as-cast (AC) condition; subsequent friction stir processing (FSP) with a tungsten-rhenium tool (shoulder diameter 12 mm, pin length 3.5 mm) at 350 RPM and 50.8 mm/min traverse speed to produce AC + FSP condition. Test conditions: In-situ tensile deformation on the VULCAN neutron diffractometer at the Spallation Neutron Source (SNS) using bulk specimens with a gauge volume of ~135 mm3. Findings: The stacking fault interspacing (LSF) decreased from an initial state to ~50 nm in the AC condition and ~10 nm in the AC + FSP condition during tensile deformation.; SF strengthening contributions (σSF) were quantified as ~50 MPa for the AC condition and ~250 MPa for the AC + FSP condition.; A sustained work hardening rate (θ) of around ~3000 MPa was observed in the AC + FSP condition, whereas the AC condition exhibited a more rapid decrease.; The decrease in LSF slowed and reached a plateau coinciding with the onset of the γ-f.c.c. → ε-h.c.p. transformation.; The AC + FSP condition showed a delayed decrease in LSF compared to the AC condition, attributed to the high density of faults formed during FSP.; The final saturated LSF of ~10 nm in the AC + FSP condition was similar to values observed in Mg alloys (~16 nm) and Co alloys (~10 nm).; The cooperative activation of SF strengthening and TRIP was evidenced by the simultaneous increase in σSF and the intensity of the ε-h.c.p. {10.1} peak.. Mechanism: Stacking faults act as barriers to dislocation motion, increasing strength as their interspacing (LSF) decreases. The onset of γ-f.c.c. → ε-h.c.p. transformation relieves stress concentrations caused by dislocation pile-ups, which explains the plateau in LSF decrease. The simultaneous activation of SF strengthening and TRIP allows for sustained work hardening and overcomes the conventional strength-ductility compromise.. Limitations: The text notes that discrepancies in measured Si and Mn content by Atom Probe Tomography (APT) are due to field ion evaporation effects, and that the study does not draw definitive conclusions regarding comparisons of TRIP HEAs with TRIP steels due to the need for additional research.. Future work: The authors state that the question of whether SFs contributed to strengthening in TRIP steels while the transformed fraction decreased with increasing strength requires additional research to draw conclusions.. Quote: "Cooperative activation of multiple mechanisms was indicated by increases in SF strengthening and γ-f.c.c. → ε-h.c.p. transformation leading to a simultaneous increase in strength and ductility."

card: Paper card. Question: What are the hot deformation behaviors, dynamic recrystallization mechanisms, and grain refinement capabilities of the Co35Cr25Ni15Mn15Fe10 TRIP-HEA under varying temperatures and strain rates?. System: Co35Cr25Ni15Mn15Fe10 (at.%) TRIP-HEA. Processing: Hot compression of cylindrical samples (12 mm height × 8 mm diameter) to a true strain of 1.0 (63% reduction) at temperatures of 1123, 1173, 1223, and 1273 K with strain rates of 0.1, 0.01, and 0.001 s−1; samples were heated to 1473 K, held for 300 s, cooled to compression temperature, held for 10 s, compressed, and water quenched.. Test conditions: Compression temperatures: 1123–1273 K; Strain rates: 0.1–0.001 s−1; True strain: 1.0; Zener–Hollomon parameter (Z) varied by temperature and strain rate.. Findings: The apparent activation energy for hot deformation was measured to be 385.7 kJ/mol.; The peak flow stress increased with an increase in strain rate and/or a decrease in temperature.; The volume fraction of dynamically recrystallized (DRX) grains ranged from 4.8% (at 1123 K, 0.1 s−1) to 82% (at 1273 K, 0.001 s−1).; The average diameter of DRXed grains ranged from 5 to 20 μm across all investigated conditions.; Discontinuous dynamic recrystallization (dDRX) was predominant at small Zener–Hollomon parameters (high temperature, low strain rate), while continuous dynamic recrystallization (cDRX) prevailed at large Z values.; A necklacelike structure composed of fine equiaxed grains and coarse elongated grains formed at medium Z values.; The constitutive equation showed a linear correlation between ln(sinh(ασ)) and lnZ with a fitting coefficient of 0.994.; Homogeneous grain structures with a size of approximately 19 μm were achieved at 1273 K and 0.001 s−1.. Mechanism: The flow softening is driven by dynamic recrystallization (both dDRX and cDRX) which consumes stored dislocation energy. dDRX nucleates at grain boundaries via bulging, favored by high temperature and low strain rates due to high grain boundary mobility. cDRX occurs via subgrain formation and rotation, favored by high strain rates and low temperatures where dislocation recovery is impeded. The high activation energy (385.7 kJ/mol) indicates sluggish diffusion, which hinders dynamic recovery and grain growth, leading to higher peak stresses and finer grain sizes compared to conventional alloys.. Limitations: The study notes that grain growth often occurs at elevated temperatures to minimize grain boundary energy, which can counteract refinement efforts at very high temperatures and low strain rates.. Future work: The study provides guidelines for optimizing grain morphology and mechanical properties of the TRIP-HEA through thermomechanical processing such as hot-compression, hot-rolling, and hot-extrusion.. Quote: "The apparent activation energy was estimated to be ~385.7 kJ/mol."

card: Paper card. Question: How can high-entropy alloy (HEA) nanoparticles be synthesized continuously and scalably directly from pure elemental metal powders without using metal salt precursors?. System: CrFeCoNiMo, CrMnFeCoNi, MnFeCoNiCu, and CrFeCoNiCu high-entropy alloys synthesized from elemental metal powders (Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, Cu, Mo). Processing: Continuous feed of equimolar elemental metal powders (1.2–2.0 g min⁻¹) into a 45 kW, ~3 MHz induction plasma jet at 66.7 kPa; vaporization in core (>8000 K) followed by rapid quenching (10⁵–10⁶ K s⁻¹) using Ar, Ar-H₂ (8.3% H₂), or Ar-He (77.4% He) plasma gases; collection via cyclone separator and porous filter (2.8 μm pore size). Test conditions: Synthesis at 66.7 kPa with plasma power fixed at 45 kW; optical emission spectroscopy at Z=0.23 m and Z=0.49 m; thermal stability tested by annealing at 1173 K (900 °C) for 72 h in flowing argon; optical absorption measured via diffuse reflectance spectroscopy from 250 to 2500 nm. Findings: Achieved continuous synthesis rate approaching 35 g h⁻¹ with a conversion efficiency of 42% for CrFeCoNiMo HEA NPs.; Produced spherical HEA NPs with average sizes of 39.7 ± 20.3 nm (Ar-He) and 60.8 ± 30.1 nm (Ar-H₂).; All synthesized HEA NPs exhibited a single FCC crystal structure despite constituent elements having BCC or HCP structures in bulk.; HEA NPs demonstrated excellent light absorption with average absorptance >96% over a wide spectrum (250–2500 nm).; HEA NPs remained thermally stable after annealing at 1173 K for 72 h, with minimal dealloying or segregation.; Mo composition in products was lower than feedstock (e.g., 5.2% in HEA-He vs. 20% in feed) due to Mo's low saturation vapor pressure.; HEA-He samples showed higher crystallinity (crystallite size 17.93 nm) compared to HEA-H₂ (17.08 nm) due to faster cooling rates.. Mechanism: The authors propose that the high-entropy effect (increased mixing entropy and decreased partial pressure of individual elements) prevents pure metal nucleation despite large nucleation temperature gaps. For hydrogen plasma, the mechanism is predominantly Vapor-Liquid-Solid (VLS) transformation where Mo nuclei form first, followed by co-condensation in the liquid phase allowing diffusion-driven alloying. For helium plasma, the mechanism is predominantly Vapor-Solid (VS) transformation due to rapid cooling, leading to direct solidification with less amorphous content but potentially higher element segregation.. Limitations: The low saturation vapor pressure of Mo leads to incomplete evaporation and compositional deviation (Mo loss) in the final product. Unvaporized feedstock powders (up to tens of μm) are generated and must be removed, reducing overall yield. Compositional variation exists among particles (up to 8.4% for HEA-H₂) due to size distribution. Cu segregation was observed at particle edges in CrFeCoNiCu systems due to positive binary mixing enthalpies.. Future work: Optimize processing parameters (feed rate, plasma power, powder injection geometry) to improve Mo evaporation and compositional uniformity. Investigate direct solar energy absorption experiments with the produced HEA NPs. Explore reactor geometries with rapid jet expansion or thermal insulators to control particle size and residence time. Study the effect of using nano-sized Mo powders to ensure better evaporation without altering the thermofluidic field.. Quote: "Here, we propose an ultrafast (< 100 ms), one-step method that enables the continuous synthesis of HEA NPs directly from elemental metal powders via in-flight alloying."

Paper card. Question: How to extract light absorptance spectra from high-entropy alloy nanoparticle samples and how reactor geometry and plasma gas composition affect the thermofluid field during synthesis?. System: High-entropy alloy (HEA) nanoparticles (HEA NP) and elemental metal feedstock. Processing: Diffuse reflectance spectroscopy using a Perkin Elmer Lambda-900 spectrophotometer with a 15 cm diameter integrating sphere; samples crushed into 1 cm diameter pellets; CFD simulations using an in-house plasma code coupled with ANSYS-FLUENT based on magneto-hydrodynamic (MHD) theory and the Reynolds stress model; DFT simulations using VASP with PAW method, GGA-PBE, 520 eV cutoff, and 100-atom supercells. Test conditions: Pellets measured with a 1 cm diameter aperture; scan rate reduced from 240 nm min−1 to 6 nm min−1 above 2000 nm and around 810 nm; DFT calculations performed at 8 different lattice constants; plasma gas properties calculated under local thermodynamic equilibrium (LTE) assumption. Findings: Diffuse reflectance (Rd) was calculated as Rd = (Is-I0)/(I100-I0) where Is is sample measurement, I0 is aperture reflectance, and I100 is spectralon standard.; Absorptance (A) was extracted using A = 1-Rd because transmittance (Td) was null for the opaque pellets.; Thermodynamic and transport properties of plasma gases were calculated under the local thermodynamic equilibrium (LTE) assumption.; Vaporization of feedstock was not taken into account in CFD simulations due to lack of thermodynamic and transport data for metal vapors in the 1000 − 10,000 K range.; Ten different random configurations for a given phase and composition were generated and examined using the hybrid Cuckoo search code.; Spin-polarized calculations were performed for both BCC and FCC phases using 100-atom supercells.. Mechanism: The authors explain that absorptance is derived from reflectance measurements on opaque pellets, while the thermofluid field is modeled using MHD theory and the Reynolds stress model to account for turbulence, though feedstock vaporization is excluded due to missing data.. Limitations: The vaporization of feedstock was not taken into account due to the lack of thermodynamic and transport data of some metal vapors for a wide range of temperature of 1000 − 10,000 K.. Quote: "The absorptance A was directly extracted using A = 1-Rd + Td = 1-Rd, where Td is the transmittance, null is our case (the pellets were opaque)."

W3193989662.title: Scalable Synthesis of High Entropy Alloy Nanoparticles by Microwave Heating

card: Paper card. Question: How can colloidal high-entropy alloy (HEA) nanoparticles with targeted equimolar stoichiometry and diameters below 5 nm be synthesized in a single step, and can this process be scaled for industrial application?. System: CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy (equimolar composition). Processing: Single-step liquid-phase, ultrashort-pulsed laser ablation of consolidated and heat-treated micropowders of the five constituent metals; low-power system: 10 ps Nd:YAG laser, 1064 nm, 100 kHz, 8.8 W, ethanol solvent, 20 mL min⁻¹ flow; high-power system: 3 ps laser, 1030 nm, 10 MHz, water solvent, 500 mL min⁻¹ flow, scanning speed 484 m s⁻¹. Test conditions: Electrochemical analysis in 0.1 M NaOH (pH 13) using a three-electrode setup with Pt counter electrode and Ag/AgCl reference; potentials corrected to RHE; linear sweep voltammetry at 20 mV s⁻¹ with electrode rotation at 1600 rpm; current densities extracted at 1.7 V vs. RHE. Findings: Colloidal HEA nanoparticles with diameters less than 5 nm were successfully synthesized, with ultrasmall NPs (2.8 nm) making up the main product by number, surface, and volume.; The process demonstrated unprecedented scalability with a productivity of 3 grams of colloidal HEA nanoparticles per hour using the high-power laser system.; The chemical composition of the nanoparticles was nearly equimolar, preserving the target stoichiometry without selective ablation of single elements.; The crystal lattice of the nanoparticles was preserved as a single fcc structure, matching the bulk HEA target, as confirmed by XRD, SAED, and HRTEM.; The synthesized nanoparticles exhibited unique redox behavior in an alkaline environment, with mass activities of 0.104 A mg⁻¹ at 1.7 V vs. RHE for water-based synthesis.; Surface segregation of Cr and Mn was observed in larger NPs (>50 nm) due to longer residence times in the low-density mixing region, leading to minor spinel oxide formation.; The synthesis process was highly reproducible, with variations of less than 10% in productivity and size distribution, and up to 12% deviation in catalytic performance.. Mechanism: The formation mechanism involves laser irradiation creating a plume and cavitation bubble; ablated species mix with liquid vapor in a supercritical state, cool rapidly (cooling rates ~10¹² K s⁻¹), and condense into NPs. Ultrasmall NPs form via nucleation and condensation in the low-density mixing region, while larger NPs emerge from a molten layer due to Rayleigh–Taylor instability. Surface segregation and oxidation occur in a late stage for larger NPs with longer residence times, while smaller NPs cool too fast for segregation.. Limitations: The presence of a minor spinel oxide phase and surface segregation of Cr and Mn in larger NPs; the complexity of assigning specific redox features to individual metals in the multi-element system; and the lack of direct quantitative surface analysis (e.g., XPS) to confirm surface compositions.. Future work: The authors propose varying the composition of the CoCrFeMnNi alloy to identify the most active composition for catalysis, extending quantitative and structural analysis of NP surfaces to investigate the origin of catalytic performance, and utilizing the method for rapid screening of different functional materials by varying alloy composition, liquid environment, and immobilization substrate.. Quote: "Herein, this study reports the single-step synthesis of colloidal CoCrFeMnNi HEA nanoparticles with targeted equimolar stoichiometry and diameters less than 5 nm by liquid-phase, ultrashort-pulsed laser ablation of the consolidated and heat-treated micropowders of the five constituent metals."

card: Paper card. Question: How can the strong immiscibility among repelling elements be overcome to synthesize high-entropy alloy nanoparticles with more than 15 elements for efficient photothermal conversion?. System: 21-element high-entropy alloy nanoparticles (FeCoNiCrYTiVCuAlNbMoTaWZnCdPbBiAgInMnSn) and series of 9-, 13-, and 17-element HEA-NPs. Processing: Arc-discharged plasma method with extremely high evaporation temperature, ultra-fast cooling (300 K and 150 K), and a vapor-pressure (V.P.) strategy to adjust powder ratios (e.g., 10x Ti/V, 0.5x Cu/Al). Test conditions: Simulated sunlight (1.0 kW m–2 to 5.0 kW m–2), pure water and saline water (3.5 wt% to 10 wt%), outdoor testing at 41.76° N, 123.42° E. Findings: 21-HEA-NPs achieved an average absorption of >92% across the entire solar spectrum (250 to 2500 nm).; The 21-HEA-NPs reached a solar steam efficiency of nearly 99% under 1 sun irradiation.; The water evaporation rate of 21-HEA-NPs was 2.42 kg m–2 h–1 under 1 sun irradiation.; Mixing entropy (ΔSmix) increased with element count, reaching 24.28 J mol–1 K–1 for 21-HEA-NPs.; Surface temperature of 21-HEA-NPs increased to ~107°C within 90 s under 1 sun irradiation.; Thermal conductivity of 21-HEA-NPs was reduced by >15% compared to 7-HEA-NPs.; In 10 wt% saline water, the evaporation rate stabilized at ~2.36 kg m–2 h–1 and efficiency at 95.52% after 100 h.; Outdoor evaporation rate reached 4.13 kg m–2 h–1 under ~0.80 sun irradiation.. Mechanism: The enhanced photothermal conversion is attributed to the coupling of reinforced d–d interband transitions (IBTs) due to fully filled energy regions around the Fermi level and the lattice distortion effect (high-entropy induced), which reduces thermal conductivity and promotes heat accumulation.. Limitations: The text notes that phase separation occurred when elements exceeded eight in previous experiments without the V.P. strategy, and that Sn and In exhibited slightly constituent fluctuation in the 21-HEA-NPs.. Future work: The authors propose that the approach opens a vast space for synthesizing ultra-mixing HEA-NPs with immiscible elements, broadening the family of HEA-NPs and providing a platform for exploring unknown properties and various applications.. Quote: "Due to the reinforced lattice distortion effect and excellent IBTs, the nanoparticles can realize an average absorption of >92% in the entire solar spectrum (250 to 2500 nm)."

card: Paper card. Question: Can microwave-synthesized FeCoNiMnCu high entropy alloy (HEA) coatings on SS-304 steel enhance surface hardness, thermostability, and tribo-corrosion resistance for use in solid oxide fuel-cell (SOFC) interconnects?. System: Fe20Co20Ni20Mn20Cu20 HEA coating on SS-304 stainless steel substrate. Processing: Ball-milling of Fe, Co, Ni, Mn, Cu powders (20 wt% each) at 200 rpm with a 5:1 ball-to-powder ratio; preheating at 100°C for 24 h; microwave hybrid heating (MHH) using a multimode applicator at 900 W and 2.45 GHz with charcoal as a susceptor; thermal exposure in air for up to 10 weeks at 800 °C. Test conditions: Hardness measured via Vickers tester (ASTM E384); corrosion tested by immersion in 3.5 wt% NaCl for 120 h (ASTM G44); wear tested via pin-on-disc (ASTM G99) at 2 m/s sliding speed, 1000 m distance, and 15 N axial load; microstructure analyzed via SEM and XRD. Findings: Average hardness increased from 210 HV (SS-304) to 325 HV (coated), representing a 54.76% improvement.; Corrosion weight loss of the 20% Fe 20% Co 20% Ni 20% Mn 20% Cu coating was 0.3004 mg after 120 h in 3.5 wt% NaCl.; A protective Cr2O3 layer and a high-entropy spinel coating of (Fe, Co, Ni, Mn, Cu)3O4 formed after thermal exposure at 800 °C for 10 weeks.; XRD analysis identified phases including Fe, FeNi3, Al2O3, NiCO, CuO, Mn2O3, (Fe,Co,Ni,Mn,Cu)3O4, and Cr2O3.; SEM images revealed a uniform cladding distribution with homogeneity in the interfacial layer.; The cladding demonstrated remarkable stability under thermal expansion studies, withstanding significant volume variations at elevated temperatures.. Mechanism: The formation of harder phases (FeNi3, Al2O3, NiCO, CuO, Mn2O3) during microwave cladding contributes to raised hardness. During thermal exposure, alloy elements react with atmospheric oxygen to form protective Cr2O3 and (Fe, Co, Ni, Mn, Cu)3O4 layers, which act as barriers against further oxidation, corrosion, and wear.. Limitations: Some cracks were observed between the cladding layer and substrate, attributed to differential cooling rates, residual stresses, and inadequate bonding.. Future work: Optimize microwave cladding parameters including temperature, metallic powder content, environmental conditions, irradiation duration, pre-heating time, separators, and susceptors to further enhance effectiveness.. Quote: "The deposited steel with 20% Fe 20% Co 20% Ni 20% Mn 20% Cu high entropy alloy (HEA) was exposed to thermal-exposure in the air for up to 10 weeks at 800 °C."

Paper card. Question: Can a microwave-synthesized Fe20Co20Ni20Mn20Cu20 high-entropy alloy coating enhance the surface hardness, wear resistance, corrosion resistance, and thermal stability of SS-304 steel for SOFC interconnect applications?. System: SS-304 steel substrate coated with a mixture of 20% Fe, 20% Co, 20% Ni, 20% Mn, and 20% Cu (Fe20Co20Ni20Mn20Cu20 HEA). Processing: Microwave cladding using microwave energy to deposit the HEA powder onto the SS-304 surface. Test conditions: Corrosion exposure: 3.5 wt.% NaCl media and air exposure for up to 10 weeks at 800 °C; Wear testing: Sliding speed of 2 m/s, sliding distance of 1000 m, and load of 15 N; Thermal expansion test: 1200 °C for 72 h duration in a muffle-furnace. Findings: Hardness of SS-304 was raised by approximately 54.76% after coating.; Wear rate of the coated sample was measured at 0.0018 mm3/m.; Coefficient of friction for the coated steel was determined to be 0.2.; Corrosion loss was reduced after thermal exposure in air for up to 10 weeks at 800 °C.; Thermal expansion test showed only a 1 mm3 variation in volume after exposure to 1200 °C for 72 h.; Protective Cr2O3 layer and high-entropy spinel coating of (Fe,Co,Ni,Mn,Cu)3O4 formed after thermal exposure.; Harder phases including Fe, FeNi3, Al2O3, NiCO, CuO, Fe2O3, and Mn2O3 were observed after microwave cladding.. Mechanism: The alloying components (Fe, Co, Ni, Mn, and Cu) serve as sacrificial anodes to shield the underlying steel and help form stable oxide scales. High-temperature exposure aids in the development of protective oxide scales that function as barriers to retard the diffusion of corrosive species. The enhanced hardness is attributed to the formation of distinct harder phases such as Fe, FeNi3, Al2O3, NiCO, CuO, Fe2O3, and Mn2O3.. Limitations: The text notes that dark spots on the corroded surface indicate localized corrosion where the coating may have been breached or performed less well due to flaws or microstructural alterations. The study also implies that electrical conductivity and area-specific resistance were not fully characterized in this specific work.. Future work: Emphasis must be contemplated on analyzing the electrical-conductivity for SOFCs interconnects applications. Emphasis must be centered on analyzing the oxidation-resistance and area-specific resistance in simulated service environments. Additional characterizations must be contemplated on the coatings before and after thermal exposure in air at 800°C. The cross-section of the coatings has been assessed to affirm the continuous and protective (FeCoNiMnCu)3O4 coating.. Quote: "The hardness has been ameliorated by about 54.76%."

card: Paper card. Question: How can the low-frequency conductivity of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) be modeled and predicted?. System: Nb-Mo-Ta-W HEA system. Processing: DC-magnetron sputtering with a working pressure of 1.5 mTorr and a 40 sccm Ar flow. Test conditions: Room temperature, various thicknesses (150 nm to 1200 nm). Findings: The conductivity of HEAs can be modulated through the cocktail effect; The plasma frequency and relaxation time are key factors in determining the conductivity of HEAs; The Nb15Mo35Ta15W35 composition exhibits high hardness and excellent conductivity; The conductivity of HEAs tends to differ by an order of magnitude compared to linear combinations of pure elements; The grain size and phase composition have minimal impact on the electrical resistivity of HEAs. Mechanism: The cocktail effect, lattice distortion, and changes in plasma frequency and relaxation time contribute to the conductivity of HEAs. Limitations: The study focuses on a specific HEA system and may not be generalizable to other systems. Future work: Further investigation of the mechanisms underlying the conductivity of HEAs and exploration of other potential applications. Quote: "The cocktail effect on the conductivity of HEA films, defined as the variation of conductivity achieved through linear combination of constituent elements, is exploited and examined"

card: Paper card. System: wear‐resistant materials, including coatings, surface textures, and bulk materials with various compositions and microstructures. Processing: various techniques, including physical vapor deposition, chemical vapor deposition, laser processing, electro processing, mechanical processing, chemical processing, plasma processing, gas nitriding, and ion implantation. Test conditions: different wear conditions, including dry sliding, micro‐abrasion, and water lubrication, with various loads, sliding speeds, and temperatures. Findings: 1.753; 2.7; 3.0; 4.6; 42.3; 72; 80; 96; the wear resistance of materials can be improved by surface engineering and matrix strengthening; the hardness of coatings is strongly related to their compositions and microstructures; the wear resistance of bulk materials can be improved by controlling compositions, designing microstructures, and adding reinforcements. Mechanism: the wear resistance of materials is influenced by various mechanisms, including lattice distortion, grain size effect, precipitation effect, grain boundary effect, dislocation or twinning effect, and the formation of tribolayers. Future work: further research is needed to develop new wear‐resistant materials and to understand the underlying mechanisms of wear resistance. Quote: "wear volume V is inversely proportional to the hardness at a given wear condition"

Paper card. Question: How do material properties such as hardness, stiffness, strength, and cyclic plasticity affect wear resistance?. System: Various materials including metals, ceramics, polymers, and composites. Test conditions: Different testing conditions including sliding speed, contact stress, and temperature. Findings: Hardness is a significant parameter in determining wear resistance; Substrate stiffness plays different roles in surface wear resistance in macro- and nanoscale domains; The wear resistance of ceramic-ceramic, ceramic-metallic, and metallic-metallic tribological systems depends on the H/E ratio; The ratio of the maximum contact stress to yield strength is a potential coefficient to assess polymer wear resistance; The wear resistance of amorphous materials is affected by the elastic mismatch between the surface and substrate. Mechanism: The authors explain that the wear resistance is influenced by the material's intrinsic properties, such as hardness, stiffness, strength, and cyclic plasticity, as well as the testing conditions. Limitations: The authors mention that there is a lack of data on the assessment of wear resistance using critical intrinsic material properties other than hardness. Future work: The authors suggest that future research should focus on the large-scale elaboration of nanostructures or phase compositions, computational modeling, and the anti-wear assessment of AM materials. Quote: "Hardness is widely accepted as a significant parameter in determining the wear resistance"

card: Paper card. Question: Is it possible to introduce short-range ordering (SRO) in high-entropy alloys (HEAs) to simultaneously enhance both ultimate strength and ductility, and what microstructures and mechanisms are required?. System: Equiatomic CoCuFeNiPd high-entropy alloy (HEA). Processing: Hybrid Monte Carlo (MC) and Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulations: MC site-occupancy swaps at 300 K and 1200 K using the Metropolis criterion, interchanged with MD relaxations (100 MC swaps followed by up to 100 MD relaxations per iteration) to optimize SRO; DFT calculations performed to validate cohesive energies.. Test conditions: Uniaxial tensile deformation simulations at strain rates of 2 × 10^8 s^-1 and 2 × 10^7 s^-1, at temperatures of 300 K and 1200 K; initial sample size 8788 atoms with lattice constant 3.6 Å.. Findings: The potential energy per atom decreased from -4.090 eV/atom (0 iterations) to -4.113 eV/atom (4 × 10^6 iterations), indicating energetically favorable SRO formation.; At 300 K, the ultimate stress increased from 3.4 GPa (no SRO) to 4.9 GPa (strong SRO), and ultimate strain increased from 6.0% to 9.6%.; SRO development led to the formation of three cluster types: FCC-preferred (FCCP), BCC-preferred (BCCP), and indifferent (IND) clusters.; FCCP clusters are primarily composed of Co (29 at%) and Ni (48 at%), while BCCP clusters are enriched in Fe (31 at%) and Pd (44 at%).; FCCP clusters withstand approximately 2 GPa/atom higher stresses than BCCP and IND clusters during deformation.; BCCP clusters undergo large plastic strain, acting as soft fillers, while FCCP clusters suffer relatively little plastic strain.; Strain-induced FCC to BCC phase transformations occurred in localized regions prior to the ultimate stress, driven by local compositional stability.; The presence of BCC-type structures prior to deformation was 2.4% for the 2 M sample and 3.0% for the 4 M sample, compared to 0% in the no-SRO sample.. Mechanism: The SRO creates a pseudo-composite microstructure where indifferent (IND) clusters act as a matrix, FCC-preferred (FCCP) clusters serve as hard fillers to enhance strength, and BCC-preferred (BCCP) clusters act as soft fillers to increase ductility. Deformation involves strain-induced FCC to BCC phase transformations prior to the ultimate stress, which increases work hardening, followed by dislocation slip within the untransformed FCC phase.. Limitations: The strain rates employed (2 × 10^8 s^-1) are very large compared with typical experiments, so the stress-strain curves should be interpreted as indicative of trends rather than quantitative values.. Future work: The authors suggest combining the SRO-based approach with larger-scale approaches (e.g., grain size, precipitates) to further optimize HEA mechanical response and exploring the effect of annealing temperature and grain boundaries on SRO and mechanical properties.. Quote: "Our results show that this HEA is energetically favorable to undergo short-range ordering (SRO), and the SRO leads to a pseudo-composite microstructure, which surprisingly enhances both the ultimate strength and ductility."

card: Paper card. Question: Can a single BCC solid solution of NbMoTaW refractory high-entropy alloy be successfully fabricated via selective laser melting (SLM) despite the high melting points of its constituent elements, and what are the resulting microstructural, mechanical, and corrosion properties compared to traditional superalloys?. System: NbMoTaW refractory high-entropy alloy (nominal equiatomic composition: Nb 99.9%, Mo 99.9%, Ta 99.9%, W 99.9%). Processing: Selective Laser Melting (SLM) using FORWEDO LM120 equipment with a 500 W fiber laser in an argon atmosphere (<20 ppm oxygen); initial parameters: hatch distance 0.1 mm, layer thickness 0.1 mm, laser power factor 0.8, scanning velocity 250 mm/s, S-cross scanning; followed by a remelting process (3 total passes per layer) to achieve a linear energy density of up to 2.83 J/mm. Test conditions: Microstructure and composition analyzed via SEM (HITACHI SU-8010) and EDS; crystal structure via XRD (Cu target, λ = 1.54 Å); microhardness measured on XY plane; corrosion resistance tested via potentiodynamic polarization in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution (scanning voltage −0.2 V to +0.2 V) and high-voltage scanning (−1.5 to +2 V). Findings: A single BCC solid solution was formed without secondary phases, with an experimental lattice parameter of 3.2034 Å.; Elements with lower melting points and densities (Nb and Mo) showed negative molar ratio deviations of up to 3.5% (Nb: −3.5 at%, Mo: −0.16 at%) compared to the nominal 25%.; The average grain size was 13.4 μm, significantly smaller than the 200 μm observed in as-cast NbMoTaW HEA.; Primary and secondary dendrite arm spacings were 6.59 μm and 1.68 μm, respectively, much finer than the 20–30 μm spacing in as-cast samples.; The average microhardness of the SLM-fabricated sample reached 826 Hv, compared to 446 Hv for arc-melted HEA and 310–437 Hv for superalloys.; The free-corrosion current (Icorr) of the NbMoTaW HEA was 8.716 × 10−11 A, which is two orders of magnitude lower than that of 316 L steel (8.815 × 10−9 A).; Visual corrosion testing showed 316 L steel suffered up to 1 mm corrosion depth, while the NbMoTaW alloy exhibited only crack extension and minor pitting.. Mechanism: The rapid solidification in SLM creates extremely high temperature gradients and cooling rates, limiting growth time and resulting in fine grains and slender dendrites. Composition deviations occur because powders with lower melting points and densities fuse first, spread over larger areas, absorb more energy, and evaporate earlier during the process. The improved hardness is attributed to grain refinement following the Hall–Petch law, while superior corrosion resistance is due to the presence of easily passivating elements (Nb, Mo, Ta) despite minor segregation.. Limitations: The ductility of the NbMoTaW HEA at room temperature remains low, and while composition deviation exists (up to 3.5%), it is noted that further study of mechanical properties is still necessary.. Future work: Further study of mechanical properties is required to fully assess the potential of the SLM-fabricated NbMoTaW HEA.. Quote: "The HEA shows an excellent microstructure, microhardness, and corrosion resistance performance compared with traditional superalloys."

card: Paper card. Question: How does varying the nickel atomic ratio (x = 1.0, 1.4, 1.8) in the AlCrFeCoNi system affect the microstructure, microhardness, and corrosion behavior in simulated body fluids?. System: AlCrFeCoNix alloys with x = 1.0, 1.4, and 1.8. Processing: Vacuum Arc Remelting (VAR) using high purity raw materials (≥99.5%), followed by flipping and re-melting 6 times under Argon; homogenization via annealing at 1100 °C for 48 h followed by water quenching. Test conditions: Immersion in Ringer Grifols solution at 37 ± 0.1 °C for one week; potentiodynamic polarization from -800 mV to +500 mV vs SCE at 1 mV/s; Vickers microhardness with 100 g load for 15 s. Findings: Hardness values decreased from 562 HV for AlCrFeCoNi to 455 HV for AlCrFeCoNi1.4 and 316 HV for AlCrFeCoNi1.8.; The pitting potential (Enp) increased with nickel content: 185 mV for x=1.0, 245 mV for x=1.4, and 385 mV for x=1.8.; Al concentration in the surface region dropped from ~10 at% to 2.57–3.03 at% after heat treatment and corrosion.; Open circuit potential increased by 30–50 mV during the first 24 hours due to passive layer growth.; The extent of interdendritic areas increased with nickel concentration, with Cr more segregated in interdendritic areas than in dendrites.; Corrosion current densities were much lower than those of 304SS, indicating higher resistance to general corrosion.. Mechanism: The decrease in hardness is attributed to the dissolution of Cr and Fe precipitates in the nickel-rich matrix, forming a continuous solid solution. The improved corrosion resistance with higher Ni content is linked to a more positive pit nucleation potential and a larger difference between nucleation and repassivation potentials, suggesting a strong tendency for pit repassivation. The formation of an Al-Ni compound after thermal treatment is hypothesized to corrode faster than the main HEA phase, leading to the observed drop in Al and Ni concentrations on the surface.. Limitations: The text does not explicitly state limitations of the study, though it notes that Ni content is not the only factor affecting corrosion, as microstructure and element distribution also play roles.. Future work: The authors propose that by manipulating the composition and structure of HEAs, their mechanical and chemical performance could be optimized to meet the requirements for their usage as novel medical instruments materials.. Quote: "Hardness values decreased as the percentage of nickel increased due to the dissolution of the precipitates in a nickel-rich matrix and consequently the formation of continuous solid solutions."

card: Paper card. Question: How can the compiled mechanical properties of high entropy alloys (HEAs) and complex concentrated alloys (CCAs) be used to assess their potential as structural materials and guide future development?. System: 370 high entropy alloys (HEAs) and complex concentrated alloys (CCAs), including 3d transition metal, refractory metal (RHEAs and RCCAs), light metal family, and bronzes and brasses HEAs/CCAs families; HEAs defined as alloys with 5 or more principal elements (5-35 at%); CCAs defined as alloys with 3 or more principal components.. Processing: Compilation of data from published reports from 2004 to 2016; density estimated using rule of mixtures (ROM): ρ=∑xiMi/∑xiVi; Young's modulus estimated using ROM for single phase solid solutions only: E=∑xiEi.. Test conditions: Uniaxial loading (tension or compression) at room temperature for 370 alloys; temperature-dependent testing for 27 refractory HEAs (RHEAs).. Findings: The database covers mechanical properties for 370 HEAs and CCAs reported between 2004 and 2016.; For 27 refractory HEAs, yield stress and elongation are provided as a function of testing temperature.; The database includes alloy composition, microstructure type, density, hardness, yield strength, elongation, ultimate strength, and Young's modulus.; Data entries are organized in a tree-like classification with four families and expanded into classes based on principal element combinations.; The database enables users to browse, search, filter, and plot material property maps using performance indices defined by M. F. Ashby.. Mechanism: The authors explain that HEAs are presumably stabilized by the configurational entropy of mixing, while CCAs encompass a broader range of alloys with single-phase or multi-phase microstructures; the database allows for the evaluation of performance indices for lighter, stronger, and stiffer structures.. Limitations: The properties are not equally populated for every alloy due to the lack of literature data.. Future work: The database can be used to represent various property spaces, calculate performance indices, and enable data mining to extract insights and uncover patterns to guide and accelerate the development of HEAs and CCAs.. card: Paper card. Question: How can a Co-Cr-Ni-based medium-entropy alloy be designed to achieve simultaneous ultra-high strength and sufficient uniform ductility by controlling composition, thermomechanical processing, and microstructural features?. System: Co34.46Cr32.12Ni27.42Al3Ti3 (in at%) medium-entropy alloy with FCC matrix and L12 precipitates. Processing: Vacuum induction melting, homogenization at 1200 °C for 2 h, hot-rolling at 1100 °C (50% reduction), cryo-rolling (CR) at 77 K to 80% total reduction, high-temperature annealing at 900 °C for 1 h (CRA), and subsequent aging at 700 °C for 4 h (CRAA). Test conditions: Uniaxial tensile testing at ambient temperature with a constant strain rate of 1 × 10−3 s−1. Findings: Achieved ultimate tensile strength (σu) of 2.2 GPa and uniform elongation (εue) of 13% in the CRAA-treated alloy.; The dual heterogeneous structure consists of a matrix with coarse grains (10–30 μm) and ultra-fine grains (0.5–2 μm).; Heterogeneous L12 nanoprecipitates range from several to hundreds of nanometers with a total volume fraction of 24.2%.; The lattice mismatch between the FCC matrix and L12 precipitates is extremely low at 0.011%.; The average size of fine L12 precipitates is 4.14 ± 0.62 nm with a number density of 3.4 × 1024 m−3.; Strengthening contributions calculated as: solid-solution (49 MPa), HDI hardening (800 MPa), and precipitation hardening (1115 MPa).; No twins or hexagonal close-packed (HCP) phase formed after deformation up to ~2.0 GPa stress.; Dislocation density in the fractured sample reached 3.83 × 1014 m−2 due to Lomer–Cottrell locks.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the superior properties to a combination of HDI strengthening from the heterogeneous grain structure, precipitation hardening from high-density coherent L12 particles, and enhanced ductility from the low elastic misfit strain of the interfaces which relieves stress concentration and prevents premature fracture, while the preservation of stacking faults and high dislocation density provides significant work-hardening.. Limitations: The text does not explicitly state limitations of the study.. Future work: The authors state that the strategy opens a new avenue for the development of promising heavy-duty structural materials and that the alloy elements and treatments can be readily accepted by industry.. Quote: "a Co-Cr-Ni-based medium-entropy alloy (MEA) with a dual heterogeneous structure of both matrix and precipitates can be designed to provide an ultra-high tensile strength of 2.2 GPa and uniform elongation of 13%"

card: Paper card. Question: How can a single-phase face-centered cubic medium-entropy alloy achieve both gigapascal yield strength and high uniform ductility without relying on second-phase heterogeneities?. System: Equimolar CrCoNi medium-entropy alloy (33.48Cr-32.46Co-34.06Ni atomic percent). Processing: Electromagnetic levitation melting, homogenization at 1,473 K for 12 h, hot forging (1,323–1,173 K), cold rolling to 0.5 mm sheets, followed by partial recrystallization annealing at 873 K for 1 h and water quenching. Test conditions: Quasi-static uniaxial tensile tests at strain rate 5 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹, room temperature (298 K) and liquid nitrogen temperature (77 K); loading-unloading-reloading (LUR) tests to measure back stresses. Findings: Yield strength (σ0.2) of ~1,150 MPa achieved with a three-level heterogeneous grain structure (HGS) spanning nanometer to micrometer scales.; Uniform tensile strain (Eu) reached 22% at room temperature, significantly higher than the ~2% Eu observed in homogeneous ultrafine-grained counterparts with similar strength.; The number density of nanograins (ρNG) increased from 4.7 grains/µm² before testing to 21 grains/µm² after deformation at 298 K and 31 grains/µm² at 77 K.; Back stress hardening accounted for over 80% of the total stress elevation observed during strain hardening from yield to ultimate tensile stress.; The strain hardening rate (Θ) exhibited a distinct upturn between 4% and 8% strain, contrasting with the monotonic drop seen in homogeneous structures.; The width of hysteresis loops in LUR tests was the largest ever recorded for any known alloy, indicating exceptionally high internal back stresses.; Corner twins evolved into nanograins during tensile straining, dynamically reinforcing the heterogeneity of the grain structure.. Mechanism: The heterogeneous grain structure induces load partitioning and strain gradient hardening, causing dislocation pile-ups at grain boundaries and generating geometrically necessary dislocations (GNDs). This creates large long-range internal back stresses that sustain strain hardening. Additionally, the low stacking fault energy facilitates the dynamic generation of twinned nanograins at grain boundaries during deformation, which further refines the structure and perpetuates back stress hardening.. Limitations: The beneficial effects of the HGS diminish if the material undergoes extended annealing toward uniform grains or if the alloy has high stacking fault energy where full dislocations dominate and recover/annihilate easily.. Future work: The authors propose that this strategy is generally applicable to other single-phase low-SFE alloys and metals to achieve simultaneous high yield strength and high tensile ductility.. Quote: "This heterogeneity results from this alloy's low stacking fault energy, which facilitates corner twins in recrystallization and stores deformation twins and stacking faults during tensile straining."

card: Paper card. Question: How can nanoprecipitates be designed and controlled in high-entropy alloys (HEAs) to achieve high strength while maintaining good ductility, and what are the specific mechanisms governing their formation and strengthening effects?. System: FCC-based HEAs including (FeCoNiCr)94Ti2Al4, Ni2CoCrFeNb0.15, Al0.3Cu0.5CrFeNi2, CoCrFeNi(Ni3Al)x, and (Ni1.5FeCoCr0.5)87.5Al7.5Ti5.0; also BCC-based systems like AlxCoCrCuFeNi and refractory systems like TaNbHfZrTi. Processing: Aging heat treatments at temperatures ranging from 550 °C to 1000 °C for durations from 150 h to 720 h; severe plastic deformation for grain refinement; mechanical alloying (MA) for high-density particle introduction; laser cladding for coatings; and direct addition of stoichiometric strengthening phases (e.g., Ni3Al) to the matrix. Test conditions: Room temperature tensile testing; compression testing; corrosion testing in NaCl and sulfuric acid solutions; hardness measurements (HV); microstructural analysis via TEM/SEM after aging; cryogenic treatment at -40 °C. Findings: The Ni2CoCrFeNb0.15 HEA aged at 650 °C for 80 h retained D022-Ni3Nb precipitates with a size of only ≈15 nm, demonstrating the slow diffusion effect in HEAs.; The (FeCoNiCr)94Ti2Al4 HEA achieved a yield strength of ≈1005 MPa and tensile strength of ≈1,273 MPa with an elongation of ≈17% due to nanoprecipitate strengthening.; In the Al0.3Cu0.5CrFeNi2 HEA, adding 0.073 at% C promoted M23C6 carbide formation, increasing yield strength by 193 MPa and ultimate tensile strength by 415 MPa while maintaining 88% elongation.; The (Ni1.5FeCoCr0.5)87.5Al7.5Ti5.0 HEA exhibited a yield strength >1.0 GPa, tensile strength ≈1.5 GPa, and elongation ≈50% due to a unique nanolamellar structure with coherent boundaries.; The Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA aged at 800 °C showed a precipitate size increase of only 6 nm (from 45 nm to 51 nm) between 50 h and 100 h aging, indicating slow coarsening.; In the CoCrFeNiMo0.3 alloy, the precipitation of fine σ and μ intermetallic phases resulted in a yield strength of 816 MPa, tensile strength of 1.2 GPa, and elongation of 19%.; The γ′ phase in HEAs can be stabilized by adjusting the Ti/Al ratio; a ratio within 0.7–2 favors L12 phase formation, while Ti/Al = 1/3 favors B2 phase formation.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the superior performance to the 'slow diffusion' effect in HEAs, which limits precipitate growth and coarsening, allowing for the retention of fine nanoscale precipitates. Strengthening mechanisms include Orowan bypass for incoherent large precipitates, dislocation cutting for coherent nanoscale precipitates (L12, D022), order strengthening due to atomic arrangement, and grain refinement strengthening where carbides suppress grain growth. The 'cocktail effect' and high mixing entropy also contribute to phase stability and the formation of simple solid solutions.. Limitations: The text states that the influence of the size and type of nanoprecipitates on the strengthening effect is still not clear, and the design method and precipitation conditions are relatively vague. Additionally, increasing the volume fraction of γ′ precipitates can increase the risk of forming harmful intermetallic compounds or cause processing problems. Over-aging can lead to the transformation of metastable phases into hard, brittle intermetallic compounds (like δ, σ, or η phases), which deteriorate mechanical properties.. Future work: The authors outline the need to further explore the effects of the types and sizes of nanoprecipitates on the strengthening effect. They propose using the OVEC (valence electron concentration) design strategy to control precipitate structures. Future work should focus on alloy-design strategies that consider the matrix composition after precipitates separate out, rather than just the initial composition, to maintain the advantages of HEAs.. Quote: "The characteristics of multiple principal elements and slow diffusion effect of elements in HEAs provide a chance to form fine and stable nanoscale precipitates, pushing the strengths of the alloys to new high levels."

Paper card. Question: How can new nanoprecipitates and strengthening mechanisms be designed to achieve high strength without sacrificing ductility in high-entropy alloys, and what are the specific characteristics required for these precipitates and their matrix?. System: Fe25Co25Ni25Al10Ti15 (FCC matrix with L12 γ' and γ* phases), Al0.7CoCrFeNi (B2 phase with Cr-rich BCC precipitates), Al0.2CrFeCoNi2Cu0.2, lightweight Al1.5CrFeMnTi (BCC matrix with L21 phase), and refractory (TiZrHfNb)98O2. Processing: Aging treatments at temperatures between 600 and 800 °C; specific examples include aging at 700 °C for 20 h or 800 °C for 1 h; solution aging followed by direct aging; annealing to change size, shape, and coherency of L21 phases; addition of 2.0 at% O to TaNbHfZrTi. Test conditions: Aging temperatures ranging from 550 to 800 °C; aging times of 1 h to 20 h; tensile testing at room temperature (yield strength 1.11 ± 0.03 GPa, ductility 27.66% ± 1.13%); diffusion couple experiments at 1273–1373 K. Findings: The Fe25Co25Ni25Al10Ti15 HEA with Ω = 1.119 and δ = 6.277 generated a γ′ phase with an L12 structure in a disordered FCC matrix.; In dual-phase FCC + B2 structures, ellipsoidal-ordered L12 precipitates with a diameter of 8 nm were observed in FCC dendrites, while BCC-structured precipitates with a diameter around 10 nm were observed in B2 dendrites.; The precipitation temperature of γ′ nano-precipitates is between 600 and 800 °C, which is higher than that of other γ′ phases (500–750 °C).; In Al0.2CrFeCoNi2Cu0.2, the L12 phase was present after aging at 700 °C for 20 h, but no nanoscale precipitation occurred after 1 h at 800 °C.; Re-precipitation of the Laves phase was detected inside grains and on grain boundaries in solution-aging samples, whereas direct-aging samples only contained γ and γ′ phases.; The tensile yield strength of the (TiZrHfNb)98O2 refractory HEA reached 1.11 ± 0.03 GPa with a tensile ductility of 27.66% ± 1.13%.; Cu-rich nanoprecipitates precipitate around 700 °C with slower kinetics compared to the L12-ordered phase.; Carbides exhibit a much wider precipitation temperature range (550–800 °C) and are more stable than other precipitates.. Mechanism: Small lattice mismatch between nanoprecipitates and the matrix reduces specific interface energy, stabilizing nanoscale size; high shear modulus and antiphase-domain-boundary energy hinder dislocation cutting, providing coherent, modulus, and ordered strengthening; high number density is achieved via low driving force of nucleation and matrix defects; twin boundaries and phase-transformation-induced plasticity absorb dislocations to improve plasticity; nanoprecipitates act as traps for irradiation-induced vacancies and interstitials.. Limitations: Comprehensive mechanical properties do not yet reach full potentials; almost all effective nanoprecipitates are derived from superalloys with no unique HEA-specific precipitates found; negative effects include nanoprecipitate coarsening or crystal-structure transformation during high-temperature service; matrix phase design for functional properties often fails to meet expected comprehensive mechanical properties simultaneously.. Future work: Explore new nanoprecipitates and strengthening mechanisms that enhance strength without sacrificing ductility; investigate the slow diffusion effect in HEAs to better understand nucleation and growth of precipitates; study the interactions between intrinsic heterogeneities and precipitates; introduce nanoprecipitates into lightweight, refractory, and radiation-resistant HEA systems; utilize high-density dislocations and modulated FCC-to-BCC transformations for strengthening.. Quote: "The new type of nanoprecipitates should exhibit a strength enhancement without scarifying the ductility."
